intro.text: Spirits tied to the heat of Torio's ground. A yoki-hijo draws them up by stacking stones and asks them to become the tools people need to survive, so spirits and yoki-hijo alike are deeply revered.
Spirits that a yoki-hijo draws up by stacking stones and binds into tools. For some 1,700 years every known spirit was held bound to the father machine, which turned their power into hion.

Splinters of Virtuosity that live underground and are drawn by thought, feeling and art. A yoki-hijo can call them with stacked stones and bind them into tools, and their power also feeds the hion lines.

description.text: The spirits are bound up with the land's strange heat and seem to be what warms the ground around Torio. How busy they are rises and falls, peaking once every thirteen years at the Festival of Reveals.
Bound spirits provide the tools Torio depends on to survive, so the spirits, and the yoki-hijo who call and bind them, are held in deep reverence.

A free spirit is a teardrop shape about as big as a head, glowing like molten metal in swirls of red and blue. It has no eyes or other features but senses what is around it, and it can talk aloud or mind to mind. Bound spirits are silent, and those held by the father machine look icy and pulse to a soundless beat.
The hijo are Splinters of Virtuosity. They dwell underground and are drawn to thoughts, emotions and art.

items.text: When the father machine was switched on, every known spirit was bound to it. For about 1,700 years they clustered around it, unable to leave, while the land cooled and the machine turned their power into hion.
At one point a few spirits slipped free and reached the people of Futinoro, an event the scholars came to call the Incident.
A spirit spoke into Yumi's mind, saying its kind were trapped as she was. She turned down the gift it offered, and it asked her to free the spirits.
Decades after the Incident, Yumi freed another spirit, and it Connected her to Nikaro.

Building hundreds of towering stacks, Yumi drew the spirits away from the machine in ever larger numbers until the last came loose. The machine stopped and fell apart, and the freed spirits thanked her.
Once free, the hijo warmed the land again, though less than before, as they chose to keep giving part of their power to the hion lines in return for viewer dramas.
Yumi once drew thirty-seven spirits in a single session of stone stacking, a record, then asked each to change into a tool a townsperson had asked for.
Yumi says a yoki-hijo usually needs around twenty stacks of about thirty stones each to call the spirits, though smaller stacks will do if they are more intricate.

Many kinds of art can draw them, though not every kind is known to. In Torio, stone stacking by a yoki-hijo was the surest way. Some spots, such as a place of ritual, work better than others, but spirits can be called elsewhere too. Once free of the machine, they also took to historical dramas on hion viewers.

To bind a spirit, a yoki-hijo gives a little of her own power along with her art and holds in her mind an image of what it should become. If this goes wrong the spirit may grow confused or flee; if it works, the stack firms up and the spirit changes. The scholars instead bind spirits by showing them pictures.

Bound spirits usually take a form of stone or metal, always in two parts, and last five to ten years; the more bound in one session, the longer they all last. Those bound by the scholars' machine are smaller, run into trouble sooner and may not last as long.
One kind splits into two palm-sized balls, one bright orange and one dull blue. Held apart they glow, which makes them a common light in Torio; touching them together puts them out.
Flyers hover on insect-like wings, about two feet across, and are steered with a handheld controller. They are used to herd plants and chase off threats.

Another kind is a pair of grotesque statues, one male and one female, linked so that moving one moves the other the opposite way. Most hold vehicles and buildings up off the hot ground, but some are set out simply to remind people that the spirits watch over them.

A spirit can Connect two people so that they trade places every day: one controls the other's body while the other goes along unseen and unheard, passing through most things, and can stray only a few yards away. The link keeps that person's memories from being tampered with.

Each sees themselves as normal, but others see and feel the body's owner, unless one has power enough to reshape the body to match their own form. The pair understand each other's languages and may share abilities, such as a yoki-hijo's.
The link is draining: the pair sleep far more than usual, settling at about twelve hours a day, and touching sends a rush of feeling and warmth between them.
The link can be cut by force, which ends the swapping, but some Connection remains: the two can still talk mind to mind and feel each other's emotions.
